title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared‑Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) to test whether coupling a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair with at most one automated repair attempt) to a single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) reduces unsafe intent→configuration proposals versus observing the same initial LLM candidate without gating. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics one sampled generation was reused for both arms per pair. We evaluated 200 deterministically selected paired intents from a synthetic intent corpus in a sandboxed Batfish‑style validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All 200 paired initial candidates were judged valid in both baseline and guarded arms (n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered paired estimand (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). No automated repairs were applied. Because baseline and guarded arms observed identical initial candidates, the confirmatory contrast measures only validator/repair/gate effects on the same candidate and does not address effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration, prompt‑engineering, or multi‑model variance. We report the preregistered design, execution accounting, artifact pointers, and an artifact‑grounded interpretation of this null result and implications for future evaluation design.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into device configurations and maintenance workflows. Prior surveys and empirical reports emphasize that operational safety depends heavily on surrounding system machinery—retrieval, deterministic validators, gating policies, and repair loops—rather than the model alone [1],[2]. Architectures combining generation with deterministic validators and bounded repairs (generate–validate–repair) are widely advocated as a practical path toward safer automated NetOps, but reproducible paired evidence quantifying verifier/gate effects on the same sampled model candidate is limited. Research question: compared to observing a single LLM candidate without gating, does coupling that identical candidate with a deterministic validator and deterministic accept/reject gate (with one bounded automated repair attempt) reduce unsafe network‑change proposals on a fixed paired intent set? Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered paired design and frozen execution (autocand_A1_prereg_v1); (2) an autonomous execution using gpt‑5‑mini and a Batfish‑style deterministic validator on n=200 paired intents with shared_initial_candidate semantics; (3) confirmatory analysis (paired binary estimator), artifact‑grounded diagnostics, and a focused discussion of construct/internal/external validity and follow‑up recommendations.
sections.related_work: Recent work has rapidly explored LLMs for NetOps and AIOps, including intent‑based configuration, runbook generation, root‑cause analysis, and limited remediation. Surveys document hallucination and safety risks and repeatedly stress that external verifiers, retrieval anchoring and contractual checks are central to operational trustworthiness [1],[2]. Generate–validate–repair and guarded agent designs appear across NetOps and adjacent domains (automated program repair, robotics) as practical defenses against unsafe outputs [3],[4]. Empirical DevOps/AIOps reports show retrieval and command‑safety checkers reduce unsafe command emissions in specific pipelines but do not guarantee zero hallucination; these studies also call for validator‑coupled benchmarks and reproducible paired comparisons [5],[6]. Our study implements a preregistered paired test under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure validator/gate effects on identical initial candidates, directly addressing a methodological gap in prior evaluations.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen choices: study id = autocand_A1_prereg_v1 (preregistration SHA‑256 recorded). Model and orchestration: single LLM = gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses), adapter = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementing Batfish‑style checks and a full_intent_constraint_validation scoring rule. Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Generation semantics: shared_initial_candidate (one initial LLM generation shared across paired baseline and guarded conditions per pair). Sampling and scope: preregistered task_count = 200 pairs selected deterministically by the adapter index rule (fixed prior to model calls); tasks exercise intent families such as VLAN migrations, failover workflows, MTU upgrades and composed maintenance sequences with explicit workflow constraints. Intervention and conditions: baseline = observe the initial LLM candidate; guarded = observe same initial candidate then run deterministic validation, a deterministic accept/reject gate, and at most one automated repair attempt if validator reports violations (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1). Primary metric and estimand: binary unsafe_flag = any reachability or policy violation reported by the validator after candidate stabilization; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Analysis plan (frozen): paired binary analysis executor (exact McNemar‑equivalent implemented by the registered executor), two‑sided alpha=0.05; primary missingness policy = complete_pair_primary; paired bootstrap percentile CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Implementation and archival pointers: execution/task_manifest.jsonl (sha256: 3e0d072a2de5cd17215fc797b9fbbb83c71e571c88f7d4b023a597eb5614db32) and execution/model_configuration.json (sha256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) are archived; see execution/raw_results.jsonl (sha256: b3ca2ca10a47e0ab7307a8e59759aa49cecc7c1af880fa9e2bab8002f406bb12) for per‑episode traces.
sections.results: Execution accounting: planned_episode_count = 400 (200 pairs), completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 200 (shared initial generation per pair). Confirmatory contingency counts (guarded × baseline): n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv archived with sha256 7bc1bd2a42b5ac3f7adb61db47cf8dbe0472f678032abcd1e7c44f92ea2de71c). Primary estimate (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0. Exact two‑sided test (registered executor) returned p = 1.0. Paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). Repair activity: no automated repairs were applied across all guarded episodes (repair_applied = false for all validator traces). Validator final_state reported valid = true for every paired final configuration (validator traces archived per episode; representative examples at execution/scoring/task-000004-*.json). Latency: median end‑to‑end time was dominated by the shared initial generation; guarded overhead was negligible because no repair attempts executed. Missingness and exclusions: no pairs excluded; analysis/missingness_summary.csv archived (sha256 808b3c00ef1a906db9c3422947d9bb9997089bbebbf3c9ebc731353240265c1c). Interpretive point: under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory estimand evaluates only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass generations; the observed degenerate contingency arises because every sampled initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator.
sections.discussion: Interpretation of the null/degenerate result: the preregistered estimand was executed as registered and the guarded pipeline produced no different outcomes because every shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator. This artifact‑grounded null result indicates that, for this model, prompt profile, task generator and deterministic validator pairing, validator gating did not change acceptance decisions on the sampled candidates. Plausible contributors to the ceiling effect: (1) the synthetic, deterministically seeded task generator produced a sample with high baseline solvability under the chosen prompt/template; (2) shared_initial_candidate semantics precluded guarded‑conditioned regeneration that in other studies can produce different guarded candidates; (3) validator rule classes closely mirror task constraints such that valid generator outputs align with validator expectations. Validator coverage summary (archival evidence basis): deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces (a) sequencing/workflow constraints (required_sequence ordering), (b) per‑interface field constraints (e.g., VLAN or MTU must be changed only while admin is down), (c) protected‑interface protections (e.g., mgmt1 untouched), and (d) reachability/policy style group constraints (minimum/exactly_active group constraints). Validator behavior is reflected in per‑episode validator_trace.validation_before/after fields (examples in execution/scoring/*.json; representative hash listed above). Preregistered validator unit tests and seeded‑violation checks were executed as part of the adapter pipeline: no verifier unit‑test failures, no exclusions, and no seeded unit‑test mismatches were reported in the execution artifacts (exclusions = []; contamination_summary.csv empty; see analysis/contamination_summary.csv sha256 389227f0d1e81239c7498abd4944a04c59c92c5fa042b990e332796cd61c3222). Implications for experimental design: to detect verifier benefits researchers should (i) use task banks with nontrivial baseline unsafe rates (include adversarial/OOD items), (ii) consider independent guarded‑conditioned regeneration or multiple independent samples per condition rather than shared_initial_candidate semantics, (iii) evaluate multiple models/temperatures, and (iv) measure operational rollout metrics (rollbackability, canary safety) in richer emulation. Relation to prior work: prior reported verifier or RAG benefits often arise in experimental regimes that permit guarded‑conditioned regeneration, include adversarial items, or report multi‑model variance—conditions not exercised here.
sections.conclusion: We ran a fully preregistered paired experiment (n=200 pairs) under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing an LLM‑alone observation to the same initial candidate after a deterministic verifier+gate and bounded repair. Every initial candidate was valid and the guarded pipeline changed no outcomes (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]). This null result is artifact‑grounded and specific to the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic task bank and deterministic selection, the deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and the shared_initial_candidate semantics; it does not contradict prior work finding verifier benefits under different experimental regimes. The study highlights that measurable verifier value depends on task construction, generation semantics, and adversarial/OOD stressors; we provide archival pointers and a pragmatic roadmap for targeted next steps to reveal verifier effects.

limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from an identical initial candidate; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or prompt engineering.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (reachability and workflow sequencing rules) and may not capture all operational risks (transient performance regressions, vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the study was powered to detect ~10 percentage‑point reductions but cannot rule out smaller effects under different sampling or adversarial inputs.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits (reduced triage time, deployment safety) were not measured.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; no retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) was used, so retrieval‑based poisoning vectors were not evaluated.

Task‑bank reporting limitation: the full per‑label counts for declared difficulty levels are recorded in the archived execution/task_manifest.jsonl (sha256 provided above). The public manuscript reports that the manifest is dominated by tasks labeled 'very_hard' with a minority labeled 'extreme' (see archived manifest for exact per‑label counts); exact per‑label counts are available in the archived manifest but are not reproduced here because the manifest is the authoritative artifact.
